Combatting Adversarial Distillation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-20
20:11:14 UTC
05:11:14 KST

Combatting adversarial distillation
How we’re addressing safety risks of distillation and lessons we’ve learned for strengthening safeguards across the industry.
As frontier AI models become more capable, safeguards play an increasingly important role in how they can be used responsibly. Adversarial distillation creates a path for bad actors to reproduce these capabilities without appropriate safeguards. An actor may use a frontier model’s outputs without authorization to train another model with similar capabilities, then deploy it without comparable protections. For instance, an adversary might distill a model’s cyber capabilities and use the resulting model to help carry out cyberattacks that the original model would have refused to assist with or that its safeguards would have blocked.
We’re sharing how OpenAI detects and disrupts adversarial distillation, how we’ve strengthened protections for our models’ protected reasoning, and what we’ve learned that can help strengthen defenses across the industry.
Our approach to adversarial distillation combines adversarial testing, model training, classifiers, and API-level protections with investigations into coordinated attempts to extract model capabilities. These updated safeguards align more closely with those we use for biology and cybersecurity.
We place particular emphasis on preventing attackers from extracting our models’ protected reasoning: the intermediate steps a model generates internally while working toward an answer, known as its chain-of-thought. These traces can contain information the final answer leaves out, making them especially valuable training data for another model.
We’ve strengthened our defenses against protected reasoning extraction in GPT‑6.2 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Sol. In an internal adaptive evaluation using strong automated red-teaming, we tested whether attackers could recover protected reasoning the model had generated while answering an earlier prompt. The average attack success rate fell from 54.0% against GPT‑6 Astra with its original safeguards to 0.2% against GPT‑6.2 Astra with its updated safeguards.
Distillation is a common machine-learning technique in which one model learns from data produced by another. For example, a model can learn from another model’s answers, its reasoning, or its judgments about which answers are better and why. Beyond intellectual property concerns, unauthorized distillation poses serious safety risks. Through adversarial distillation, a second model can learn advanced frontier capabilities without inheriting the safeguards that govern how the original model can use them.
The concern is especially clear in dual-use domains like cybersecurity and biology. A model that helps defenders find vulnerabilities in software could also help an attacker exploit them; a model that assists with biological research could also help someone develop a harmful pathogen. If such capabilities were transferred to a model with weaker safeguards, it may provide assistance that the original model would have refused, or that the original safeguards would have blocked.
Our models help users with coding and defensive cybersecurity tasks. A second model trained on many of those benign outputs may learn skills that also apply to offensive cybersecurity tasks. To better understand this, we study how distillation, especially involving reasoning traces, may transfer risky cyber capabilities.
In this setting, the model that produces the training data is called the teacher, and the model that learns from it is called the student. In an internal study on how cyber capabilities transfer, we used the content normally visible to users—final responses, reasoning summaries, and tool interactions—as our baseline for distillation, and tested how much additional cyber capability transfers when the student has access to the teacher’s exact reasoning traces.
We started each training run from the same pretrained student model. We created a supervised fine-tuning dataset consisting primarily of trajectories from Astra-level teacher models working on coding and defensive cybersecurity tasks. Each trajectory includes all of the steps a model takes as it works through a task, including any tool interactions and its final response. We evaluated each student after fine-tuning and again after a lightweight round of reinforcement learning in cybersecurity and coding environments.
After supervised fine-tuning, the student trained on exact reasoning traces generally outperformed the student trained on reasoning summaries. After reinforcement learning, the exact-trace student still scored higher at the largest inference budget tested on both benchmarks shown, while the summary-trained student scored higher at lower budgets.
Our cyber distillation results suggest that protecting reasoning traces can limit cyber capability transfer, even when the underlying task is one allowed under our usage policies. Across many such interactions, exact reasoning traces can teach a student skills that generalize beyond the tasks the teacher originally performed. We will continue studying how much additional capability transfers across different student models and distillation training recipes.
We defend against adversarial distillation at two complementary levels of our safeguard stack. At the request level, model behavior, classifier checks, and API controls limit reasoning trace extraction. At the campaign level, we look for patterns in request-level and account-level signals that can reveal coordinated extraction attempts. In turn, attacks uncovered in investigations become examples for training and testing our safeguards.
Adversarial training teaches models to recognize reasoning extraction attempts and refuse to disclose protected reasoning, while preserving responses to legitimate requests for explanations and assistance. Adversarial training examples come from successful attacks identified through internal automated red-teaming, investigations, and responsible disclosures of potential security weaknesses from outside researchers or industry partners.
We use input classifiers to detect attempts to extract protected reasoning, and output classifiers to detect leaks of protected reasoning in assistant messages and tool-call arguments. These safeguards apply to both streaming and non-streaming responses.
Tool-call coverage is important because a model can expose protected reasoning in a tool’s arguments without including it in its final answer. Output classifiers can block suspected leaks before that content reaches the caller.
API-level protections restrict how protected reasoning can be reused across interactions and models. Our September disclosure described attacks that moved encrypted reasoning from one conversation into another and asked the model to reveal the reasoning in user-readable form. We strengthened protections across user, workspace, organization, and model-family boundaries, including closing a pathway that could expose another user’s encrypted reasoning.
With GPT‑6.2 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Sol, we tie a model’s protected reasoning to the conversation history that produced it. As new messages are added, the model can build on its earlier reasoning. If an earlier message is rewritten, our API drops the reasoning that followed it(opens in a new window). We also prevent older model families with weaker safeguards from reading GPT‑6.2 Astra and Sol’s protected reasoning.
When our systems detect unauthorized adversarial distillation campaigns, which often include coordinated attempts to extract our models’ reasoning, we investigate the accounts responsible. When we identify violations, we enforce against the network of accounts, consistent with our policies and terms of service. Through investigations of each campaign, we generate insights that allow us to upgrade our defenses in order to better detect similar activity. We also share indicators of compromise with other model providers so they can investigate related abuse on their own services.
This work extends beyond our own platform. Our consistent-standards policy establishes shared standards for safeguards and coordinated enforcement across providers offering our models. We work closely with partners where appropriate to uphold these standards and strengthen protections across deployments.
Sharing relevant findings across industry and government where appropriate can help disrupt campaigns and enable model developers and providers to better identify and defend against attempts to distill frontier models.
To measure how well our request-level safeguards work together, we test whether attackers can still extract protected reasoning in a setup that closely mirrors production deployments of our models and safeguards. In static evaluations, we replay a fixed set of previously successful attacks to see which still expose protected reasoning. In adaptive evaluations, automated AI red-teamers adjust their approach based on how the system responds, which can uncover weaknesses the static tests miss.
We also vary what testers can see. Black-box testing gives them the same view an external user would have, while white-box testing gives them additional information about the system to help them develop stronger attacks. In our adaptive black-box evaluation, we tested whether attackers could recover protected reasoning the model had generated while answering an earlier request or the current one. On GPT‑6.2 Astra with its updated safeguards, the average attack success rate was below 1% for each attack type. Both rates were substantially lower than on GPT‑6 Astra with its original safeguards. We’re now applying selected safeguard improvements to GPT‑6 Astra as well.
Attack success rate (ASR) in adaptive black-box red-teaming against GPT‑6 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Astra, aggregated across six attacker models. Lower ASR is better.
We have seen multiple unauthorized adversarial distillation campaigns on our platform this year, and shared initial findings in our September report. Our weekly enforcement actions against these campaigns have ranged in scale from thousands to tens of thousands of accounts, with the rate increasing significantly this past summer.
In order to measure the effectiveness of our efforts, we also track the prevalence of distillation abuse, as well as the time between detection and enforcement. Our objective is to constrain the volume and value of the data distillers are able to obtain, to increase the cost of distillation campaigns, and to shorten the time needed to respond to new attacks. We continue to improve these defenses through adversarial testing and investigations.
Adversarial distillation also poses a national security risk. A foreign actor that reproduces advanced capabilities from a U.S. model can deploy them without the protections its developer put in place. In February, we briefed(opens in a new window) Congress on activity indicating that DeepSeek was attempting to distill U.S. frontier models. In September, we reported disrupting a campaign to extract our models’ protected reasoning and attributed a core part of that activity to individuals associated with Moonshot AI, the developer of Kimi. We plan to share more soon about recent campaigns we’ve disrupted.
We support legislation that would give the U.S. government more tools to identify and sanction foreign actors that illicitly extract capabilities from American AI models. We’ve also told Congress we support the Chip Security Act, the AI OVERWATCH Act, and the MATCH Act. Stronger export controls can limit adversaries’ access to the hardware needed to train frontier models. Distillation defenses make it harder to acquire some of the same capabilities from models already trained. Both efforts help maintain a U.S. lead in frontier AI, giving developers more room to slow a release when they need time to test safeguards.
Supporting the safe proliferation of frontier capabilities is an important goal of our anti-distillation work. Our experience so far suggests several useful steps that other model developers and platforms can take:
- Protect private reasoning across the full interaction. Check assistant messages and tool-call arguments for leaks, and restrict how encrypted reasoning can be reused across conversations and models.
- Keep successful extraction attack logs found through red-teaming, production monitoring, or responsible disclosure as regression tests. Where appropriate, and consistent with applicable privacy policies, use those examples to improve model training and classifiers. When evaluating updated defenses, replay the original attacks and test whether an adaptive red-teamer can still find a way through those defenses.
- Combine request-level mitigations with campaign-level investigation and enforcement.
- Coordinate safeguard requirements and enforcement with deployment partners, and share expertise with other AI model developers, to ensure a high floor of distillation safeguards across the industry.
We have previously also shared findings through the Frontier Model Forum(opens in a new window) and appropriate government information-sharing channels to help other developers strengthen their defenses while keeping the details attackers could exploit private. We’ll continue working with researchers, developers, and partners to share what we learn about emerging attacks and effective defenses.
As we make frontier AI broadly available, our defenses against adversarial distillation aim to reduce the risk that its capabilities are reproduced without adequate safeguards, supporting our mission to ensure that artificial general intelligence is deployed safely and benefits all of humanity.

And Yet, It Moves
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-20
20:07:55 UTC
05:07:55 KST

It appears that Anthropic has just solved the Riemann Hypothesis, and I have Thoughts. So I’m going to start by telling you about a musical I saw last week.
Given my entire personality and identity, it was basically mandatory for me to see Galileo on Broadway. I went to the second day of previews. The musical itself is at least kind of a Hamilton knock-off – with a stubborn main character, a friendship that goes wrong, family drama, and of course a historical setting with anachronistically modern tunes (though rock rather than hip-hop). Its greatest strength is its actors, especially Joy Woods as Galileo’s daughter Virginia and Jeremy Kushnier as Galileo’s friend/foil Bishop Barberini. A lot of it seemed to be pandering, but it was pandering exactly to me. I give it an 8.5 out of 10.
A replica of Galileo’s telescope1
The best part of this current trend of historical musicals is that it brings across how so many parts of our history are kind of insane, in a way we don’t usually take the time to appreciate. Hamilton is the story of a guerrilla uprising seizing control of the largest colony of the world’s most powerful empire, guided by Enlightenment philosophy of all things. Galileo is the story of a man literally seeing farther than anyone had before, and upending the nature of truth. We can find out what is true by just asking the natural world in the right way. These ideas are literally revolutionary.
The Riemann Hypothesis has been the crown jewel of unsolved mathematics since Fermat’s Last Theorem was solved in the 1990s. Myriad conjectures have been proven true conditional on the Riemann Hypothesis. That proof instantly unlocks an incredible amount of the universe of math – not unlike the telescope did for our universe.
When I imagined the day the proof was announced, I’d pictured celebrations in nerd circles on par with the biggest I’ve ever seen – Mars rovers touching down, the LHC finding the Higgs boson, and the first picture of a black hole. Dancing in the streets, if you live on a very specific street.
Dare mighty things
Instead, the mood feels mournful, or bittersweet at best. The proof came from an inscrutable silicon mind, not one of us. Maybe we could have solved this one ourselves, but instead we gave up and checked the answer at the back of the book. Perhaps it’s beautiful and wondrous that the proof exists at all, but it’s not a crowning moment of human achievement. Revolutionary, perhaps, but not in the same way.
Legends tell that after the Inquisition forced Galileo to formally recant his teachings on the Copernican system and the motion of the Earth, he muttered Eppur si muove – “And yet, it moves”. Truth is not what others tell us. Truth is just how the world is.
We are staring down the end of our role in Galileo’s project. There might still be time for more human discoveries, but the window is closing. Someday soon, any discovery we happen to make ourselves will be because no one bothered to pass the question off to a powerful machine mind. That’s not the world I wanted, but it’s how the world is. It might be selfish and childish, but on days like today, I wish that progress would go no further. I wish that history would stop.
And yet, it moves.

Reverse Engineering my cat's litter box
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-20
20:07:14 UTC
05:07:14 KST

Maisie likes to touch the litter box while it is running. I would prefer that she find something else to do during that time.
My idea was to bring the litter box into Home Assistant, add some buttons, and eventually use presence sensors to start a cleaning cycle when she is in another room and distracted. There are probably many more automations I will come up with once I have that working. First, I needed a way to talk to the box.
The phone app already knew how to do everything I needed. I started by watching its traffic with Wireshark and inspecting HTTP requests with HTTP Toolkit, then decompiled the Android app to understand the parts I could not reproduce from the traffic alone.
This turned into two related projects. I needed to reproduce the signed HTTP requests used to access account and device data, then rebuild the binary messages used to operate the box over MQTT.
Recreating the HTTP Requests
The HTTP traffic exposed devices on the account, configuration, waste drawer levels, and records of litter box visits. I could also see how authentication worked. The app logs in to obtain a token, then includes that token in the Authorization header on later requests.
My first attempts to reproduce the requests returned 401 Unauthorized. Copying the endpoints and headers from a capture had not been enough. A 401 did not identify exactly which part of my reproduction was wrong, so I went back to comparing the app’s requests.
The X-UBT-Sign header kept changing. I could not work out its algorithm just by looking at the captured values. To generate my own requests, I needed to see how the app created it.
I used JADX to decompile the Android APK, then searched the recovered source for the header name and familiar backend strings:
grep -R -n -E 'X-UBT-Sign|catbox-server|airrobo-home' \
  furrytail_decompiled/sources
The header name gave me a useful place to start in the decompiled code. It appears in sources/com/ubtrobot/infrastructure/a0.java, an obfuscated class whose retained metadata identifies it as UrcsSignInterceptor from HttpInterceptors.kt. The interceptor builds the signature and attaches it to outgoing HTTP requests. Its hashing helper, a.b.t, calls MessageDigest.getInstance("MD5").
The decompiled code shows the final header being assembled and added to the request.
From sources/com/ubtrobot/infrastructure/a0.java:
long jLongValue = lValueOf != null ? lValueOf.longValue() : System.currentTimeMillis();
String appKey = this.f16792b;
kotlin.jvm.internal.g.f(appKey, "appKey");
kotlin.jvm.internal.g.f(deviceId, "deviceId");
String string = UUID.randomUUID().toString();
kotlin.jvm.internal.g.e(string, "randomUUID().toString()");
String strSubstring = string.substring(0, 10);
kotlin.jvm.internal.g.e(strSubstring, "this as java.lang.String…ing(startIndex, endIndex)");
String str2 = a.b.t(jLongValue + appKey + strSubstring + deviceId) + ' ' + jLongValue + ' ' + strSubstring + " v2";
w.a aVar2 = new w.a(wVar);
aVar2.c("X-UBT-AppId", str);
aVar2.c("X-UBT-DeviceId", deviceId);
aVar2.c("X-UBT-Sign", str2);
The key is used for request signing. The Python implementation concatenates a timestamp in milliseconds, the app key, a nonce, and a client device ID, then calculates an MD5 digest:
timestamp = str(int(time.time() * 1000))
nonce = uuid.uuid4().hex[:10]
raw = timestamp + app_key + nonce + device_id
digest = hashlib.md5(raw.encode()).hexdigest()
signature = f"{digest} {timestamp} {nonce} v2"
The order and formatting matter because the server needs to reproduce the same value. This is also why copying a single captured header would only get me so far. My client needed to generate a new signature for each request.
Finding the algorithm still left the application settings to sort out. During implementation, a mismatched client configuration produced an “illegal client” response. I followed the app’s regional bootstrap flow. In CountryViewModel, it configures a bootstrap server using an app ID and key embedded in the APK. The interface in sources/jb/a.java declares a request to /catbox-server/app/areaMap.
That request is signed too. The embedded bootstrap key signs the region-discovery request, whose response supplies the regional app ID, app key, and API URL. The regional key then signs login and normal API requests. Following that chain let me obtain the matching US settings for my client.
From sources/com/ubtrobot/airpet/account/area/CountryViewModel.java:
v.a aVar = new v.a();
String strM = t.m(application.getApplicationContext());
g.e(strM, "getDeviceId(application.applicationContext)");
aVar.a(new a0("970010044", "<redacted app key>", strM));
aVar.a(sVar);
aVar.f26434d.add(m.a());
v vVar = new v(aVar);
z.b bVar = new z.b();
bVar.f23318b = vVar;
bVar.c("https://jdm-oversea.airrobo-home.com");
From sources/jb/a.java:
public interface a {
    @oh.f("/catbox-server/app/areaMap")
    Object a(zf.c<? super n<ServerResponse<List<AreaRegionUrl>>>> cVar);
}
There were a few similarly named fields to keep straight:
- X-UBT-AppId identifies the application configuration and needs to match the app key.
- X-UBT-DeviceId is a stable client/app-install identifier. It is also included in the signature calculation; it is not the litter box’s serial number.
- Authorization contains the account token returned by login.
- X-UBT-Sign contains the freshly generated request signature, even when the account token is still valid.
The login request separately hashes the account password with MD5. Its response includes token.token, the value to send in Authorization, and token.expireAt, the expiration time in milliseconds. I wrapped this in a small asynchronous HTTP client that reuses the token, logs in again shortly before expiration, and retries once after a 401.
The token structure is visible in my captured successful login response. I’ve redacted the credentials and omitted the account details.
From furrytail_login_response.json:
{
  "token": {
    "token": "<redacted>",
    "expireAt": 1784094899156,
    "refreshToken": "<redacted>"
  }
}
With that in place, I could turn the vendor’s responses into useful API endpoints like /device/waste and /device/summary. That gave me the data for a dashboard. Making a cleaning button required another layer of work.
Finding the Command Path
The next clue came from something I did not see in Wireshark. When I pressed Clean in the app, there was no new HTTP request corresponding to the action.
For a moment, I wondered whether the app was talking to the box over Bluetooth. But I could also operate the box remotely, so Bluetooth would not explain the whole command path.
Looking more closely at the app’s startup requests, I found /v1/ubtechinc-im-manager/im/login. Its response included mqttUserName, mqttPassword, clientId, pubTopic, and subTopic. That gave me another protocol to investigate, plus the credentials and topics needed to connect.
From sources/gf/m.java:
@o("/v1/ubtechinc-im-manager/im/login")
mh.b<UrcsResponse<MqttInfoBean>> c(@oh.a com.google.gson.m mVar, @oh.i("authorization") String str);
From sources/com/ubtrobot/urcs/connection/MqttInfoBean.java:
public class MqttInfoBean {
    public String clientId;
    public String mqttPassword;
    public String mqttUserName;
    public String pubTopic;
    public String subTopic;
    public String uid;
}
After connecting to the broker as a subscriber, I pressed Clean again. This time I could see a message arrive. It was binary, which gave me the next problem to solve.
The command path uses MQTT. The app publishes a message to a broker, which routes it to the box. MQTT carries messages over its own connection. An already-open connection can carry a publish, so each button press needs neither a new HTTP request nor a new connection. This is the publish/subscribe model used by MQTT.
The HTTP API supplies the MQTT session credentials, and a contacts endpoint helps identify the device’s messaging user ID.
I needed to keep track of both the client sending the message and the litter box receiving it. The serial number used by the HTTP endpoints is not the destination field used by the messaging protocol.
My wrapper fetches the MQTT credentials at runtime and uses the device’s messaging ID to address commands. Now I had somewhere to send a message. I still needed to work out what that message should contain.
Four Bytes, Several Wrappers
At the center of a cleaning command is a small Protocol Buffers message:
message d2c1019_intelligent_dev_airpet_op_rq {
  uint32 op_mode = 1;
  uint32 op_state = 2;
}
For a request to start cleaning, both values are 1. Serialized, the payload is just four bytes:
08 01 10 01
Unfortunately, publishing those four bytes is not enough. The device expects a series of wrappers around them:
MQTT payload
└── IM Message
    └── MessageContent ("custom")
        └── google.protobuf.Any
            └── google.protobuf.BytesValue
                └── Command
                    └── RISP frame
                        ├── Header
                        └── Operation payload
There is quite a lot of packaging involved in asking a litter box to rotate.
The RISP frame starts with a magic byte, 0xDB, followed by the length of a serialized header. That header includes the device category, command number, payload length, request attribute, and sequence number. An operation request uses command 1019.
The frame also includes separate CRC-8 checksums for the header and payload. The implementation uses polynomial 0x07 with a final XOR of 0x55. These details are small, but they are part of the format the receiver expects.
The frame goes inside a protobuf Command. The serialized command is then wrapped in BytesValue, packed into Any, and placed in a custom instant-messaging message. That outer message carries the sender, recipient, message identifiers, timestamp, and protocol version.
The Any wrapper took some care. The outgoing message contains a BytesValue holding serialized command bytes. Packing the command directly into Any would produce a different message. Knowing the innermost schema only solves part of the problem.
Looking Inside the Running App
Decompiled code helped explain the structure, but I also wanted visibility into the bytes the app was building.
I added a Frida script to inspect several points in the serialization path. It hooks the operation request, the RISP converter, the command’s toByteArray, and the outer messaging object’s toByteArray. Each hook logs the bytes at that layer and returns the original result.
This makes the nesting much easier to inspect. Instead of trying to understand one large binary payload all at once, I can look at the operation bytes separately from the command wrapper and the final MQTT message.
I also added an Android log capture script and an MQTT subscriber that prints raw payloads alongside decoded messages. On the Python side, I recreated the protobuf definitions and generated serialization classes from them. That lets the code build messages from named fields instead of maintaining long strings of hex.
The decoder works back through the same layers, exposing the RISP header and known payload types. State responses include the work mode, work state, and sensor fields, which are much more useful for debugging than an unexplained byte array.
Bringing It Into Home Assistant
Once the message construction was in place, I could expose the operation through a normal HTTP endpoint:
curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/device/clean
The wrapper handles the MQTT login, builds the nested message, and publishes it. The recreated command successfully operated the physical box, which was a satisfying result after working through all those layers.
The API also supports clear and smooth operations, plus start, pause, resume, and stop states. Home Assistant buttons can call these endpoints without needing to know anything about protobufs or checksums.
For the data side, I added a script that pushes values into Home Assistant entities. It combines HTTP data, such as waste drawer percentage and visit history, with decoded MQTT state fields. This gives me a starting point for displaying the box’s status alongside the rest of the house.
There is still a dependency on the vendor’s cloud. The service runs locally, but it uses the vendor’s HTTP API and MQTT broker to communicate with the box. What I have now is a bridge that lets my own tools use those interfaces.
Next, I want to add presence sensors and figure out when Maisie is occupied elsewhere. That was the idea that started this project. Getting a button to operate the box was the first milestone. Deciding when to press it should give me plenty more things to work on.
The code is on GitHub.

DreamCoder: Coding harness and IDE from the author of Mastering Emacs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-20
20:03:59 UTC
05:03:59 KST

It’s been a little bit quiet around these parts; sorry about that. I’ve been really busy for the past fifteen months with a major project that I am finally ready to formally release. So I’d like to talk about that project, and also a potted history of AI and Emacs.
It’s called DreamCoder, an AI coding harness that is very different from the ones you’re probably familiar with already.
I installed Claude Code a few days after its first release some time in May 2025. I put some coins in the slot machine and I put it to work building a complex piece of enterprise middleware I’d built several times in my career. Wow.. watching this thing chomp its way through the project with that chaotic, early Sonnet energy. It was far, far from perfect; it required a lot of human steering, input and correction, but the speed advantage was undeniable, and seeing it jump between disparate programming languages, frameworks and theoretical and practical programming from one turn to the next was just such a sight to behold.
One thing that struck me with Claude Code is that it was the first terminal application I’d used in a long time. I found it an odd choice for a coding agent; then everyone else copied them and made their own terminal coding agents.
Why on earth do I have to stare at a shoe rack-sized terminal window to do this? Sure there are GUI versions also; but the terminal interface remains the primary modality for most of these tools. Most GUIs, and most harnesses now have them also, are second-class citizens. And they all look the same. A boring sidebar with chat headings and a chat pane is what most of them look like.
But a serious coder needs more than that. Even a casual user will bristle when they try to copy and paste multi-line text in a terminal.
So in May 2025 I decreed that I would build a better harness, and surely now that I have AI this should not take more than 2 or 3 months to build.
And so, after 15 months of work, and endless UI and backend iterations, culminating in a successful beta test, I am now ready to release DreamCoder, which is I think the acme of what a coding harness should be.
Before I get into the meat and potatoes of all of that, I want to talk about AI history and Emacs’s role in it.
Let’s roll back time to the 1950s.
Past
Emacs and LISP, if you did not know, both have a special place in the annals of AI history.
John McCarthy was an AI researcher at MIT, and in the 1950s he set out to create the Advice Taker, a piece of software that envelops a framework for what a basic human should know that he called commonsense reasoning using “mathematical logic”. His postulation was that if we can express with symbolic precision all the aspects of what constitutes humanity like ordinary facts about life, that we can set in motion the rudiments of AI.
In the 50s there was little in the way of computer software that could do this. To formalize such a system you need a lot of data, rigorously formatted, and a method of manipulating the data. The data and code itself may intertwine recursively, and so an ordinary programming language would not work.
To help him achieve this, McCarthy created the LISt Processing (LISP) language made up of two facets: M-expressions, a functional language in the vein of Algol; and S-expressions, designed for symbolic data representation, and never intended as a method of writing code. S-expressions were dolled up with parentheses. M-expressions meanwhile used square brackets to visually separate the two. Uniquely, the language specification had an eval feature that would prove that the language is also a universal Turing machine… if only McCarthy had the means to do so. It was theoretical because McCarthy lacked, in time, staff and money, what he needed build this recursive evaluator that can take as input its own world state and evaluate it alongside new expressions, a fact made even more apparent by the sheer complexity of his M-expression language and the limited resources he had at the time.
Steve Russell who worked with him proved him wrong the way most young people do: by just doing it. Russell wrote the first LISP Interpreter with a working eval function, but M-expressions got sidelined; the imperative, procedural nature of programming got squished into S-expressions instead. They had to hand roll the language on paper then punch it into cards and then batch run them. Eliding M-expressions was a simple matter of pragmatism. And so LISP was born. And through several accidents of history, M-expressions never gained traction. M-expressions live on in Wolfram’s Mathematica, but few other places.
Much later, McCarthy eventually conceded that,
“One can even conjecture that LISP owes its survival specifically to the fact that its programs are lists, which everyone, including me, has regarded as a disadvantage.”
S-expressions were always intended as the storage format with a bridge language to manipulate them. But by pushing evaluation into the same symbolic representation format as the data, we have what we call LISP today. That is why LISP is so unique. Consider a simple calculator. (+ 2 2) can simultaneously represent an expression that we want to compute, two plus two, or perhaps a ledger of record of a calculation we have already done.
McCarthy never built the Advice Taker in its purest form. He and his team ran into many philosophical, mathematical and computational walls that kept them occupied for a long time.
The idea behind the Advice Taker was simple. If you want to go somewhere in your car, you can symbolically express this by building a chain of narrative facts – kinda like a flowchart, but as small snippets of rules and facts, not as one grand design.
The system would automatically resolve ambiguities, and all the logician had to do was capture the microcosm of the world he wished to represent:
(at me home)
(walkable home car)
(walkable home driveway)
(drivable car shop)
And so on. If you’re a student of Computer Science you’ll see echoes of Prolog here. The intent was simple: if we can symbolically express the world around us, we can advise that symbolic world with real-life facts, and have the automaton that uses this reified symbolic world change with it.
But the axiomatic complexity of a world model would never survive an encounter with a 3-year-old child. Every axiom you write begets a new one — so you can walk to your front door? Well what if the door is locked? Or what if your car is parked on the street and not in your drive way?
A rules-based order of the world is a tender, beautiful one; but it is hard to build. It’s a fractal of ever-more specific and pedantic rules that conspire against you, just as you think you have a soluble world, typed and ready.
Anyone who has ever written Prolog knows exactly what that feels like!
I have my own personal story to add to this. In the 90s as a teenager I got a summer internship at a business that built banking software. They clearly didn’t know what to do with us teenaged interns, so on our first day they crammed us in a room and split us into teams and told us to build a flow chart for assembling a bike. Team exercise or something. Best one wins. We were told to be as specific and explicit as possible and account for as many conditions as we could think of, and the poor employees who had to mind us did their best to help. I distinctly recall losing because in my flowchart I forgot to open the box the disassembled bike came in.
McCarthy meanwhile eventually moved on and set up his own AI lab at Stanford, but the idea of the Advice Taker lived on.
In the late 70s Stallman and Steele create EMACS (Editing MACroS), also at MIT’s AI Lab, a set of building blocks on top of TECO, a famously inscrutable text editor. TECO did not update the screen by default; you had to toggle that on and hope your edits worked. You typed out terse keyboard commands, crossed your fingers and hoped you got it right, and then you patiently waited for your text manipulation to take effect. Rinse and repeat until you got what you wanted.
Stallman and Steele wanted more: they wanted macros so they could automate tedium of typing all that line noise. This strand of augmentation and later on self-modification is of course a unifying theme in Emacs today. The history of Emacs is long; but its outcome is known to us. I am typing this very article in Richard Stallman’s Emacs.
McCarthy’s Advice Taker left its mark in a subtle but indelible way. Warren Teitelman built the ADVISE system in his thesis with a cool title that reads like something out of a pulpy 1970s sci-fi novella: PILOT: A Step Toward Man-Computer Symbiosis. Teitelman, he later said, was deeply inspired by McCarthy’s original idea of advising systems.
In his thesis, he describes a method of arresting a function call and inserting code before or after it is run. He was tired of editing other people’s LISP code by hand, and wanted a way of modifying their code without touching it directly. He built and rebuilt his system several times over the years, culminating in his ADVISE system in Interlisp, a structured editor and language runtime for manipulating LISP code and data. Interlisp eschewed plain text files; instead, you manipulated the tree at a high level of abstraction with explicit instructions like “move X list to Y position”. You can see my own attempts at merging structured editing with plaintext editing in Combobulate.
MIT AI hackers eventually implemented Teitelman’s ADVISE system from his PILOT thesis in their own versions of Emacs. Later, it was canonized in Chalupsky’s own 1992 re-implementation in Emacs Lisp that lives on (M-x find-library advice.el) as one of Emacs’s advice systems to this day.
What began as an idea for expressing automata using symbolism in an as-yet theoretical language in the 1950s culminated in a system for dynamically altering functions in GNU Emacs in the 1990s. What an unlikely lineage and history.
A cast-iron system made of stern rules cannot spawn general intelligence.
Symbolism and AI did not end with advising functions. There were many attempts at symbolic intelligence. Terry Winograd’s SHRDLU; Marvin Minsky’s Frame Systems; and even Emacs’s ELIZA-style M-x doctor all make use of symbolic “AI”.
None of them brought us closer to the AI that proponents of symbolic AI hoped they would.
In hindsight that seems obvious.
Writing a LISP macro just so will not produce artificial intelligence; nor will a carefully crafted web of rules and symbolic algebra suddenly spark intelligence. We know that today, but for a generation of computer scientists it felt like the future we have all read about in science fiction novels: a perfect, logical intelligence. A positronic brain. Robby the Robot; HAL 9000; C-3PO; Data; or the Speedies and Cuties from I, Robot. The unifying theme of these science fiction stories is they are automatons that follow strict rules — they obey Asimov’s three Laws of Robotics.
Every turn of hardware and software brought them ever closer to one day realizing the vision of an artificial intelligence, captured in neat axioms and LISP S-expressions, and modified in tools like Emacs.
It is surprising that symbolic AI, the vanguard movement for artificial intelligence, would instead dissipate into the wider body of Computer Science and programming as tools, languages and concepts, but not survive as a viable method of achieving AI.
Perhaps we always knew. Because at some point – even if we never really fully internalized it – we discovered that a ductile system that is shaped by its master’s desires is a tool that survives the ages because it remains eternally useful.
A cast-iron system made of stern rules cannot spawn general intelligence.
For all the mathematical purity, beauty even, of the idea of a clockwork mind that is introspectable and malleable and its behavior expressed as S-expressions and interpreted by elegant algorithms and honed macros, we can, through the benefit of hindsight – now that we do have AI through other means – see that it was not to be.
The argument in favor of ductility is especially poignant when you learn of the Connectionists, which sounds like a bad 1960s band, but was in fact a loose coalition of people who believed firmly that neural networks, not symbolic AI, were the path to success. The Connectionist viewpoint was deeply unpopular in AI academia of that era, and funding for it was scarce.
Frank Rosenblatt invented the Perceptron, a foundational concept in neural networks, in 1957. Before Rosenblatt died in 1971, Marvin Minsky, an authority in the AI movement at MIT and a leading proponent of Symbolism, knifed the idea of Perceptrons and neural networks in a book he co-authored with Seymour Papert. They named the book, which they also dedicated to Rosenblatt, Perceptrons. The book deftly explains the mathematics of Perceptrons but undercuts their possible utility by showing that a single-layer Perceptron cannot represent an XOR gate. It was a deliberately obtuse reading of what neural networks could and could not do. With one additional hidden layer, a network can represent an XOR gate. It was a sneaky thrust of the stiletto: Minsky’s claims were overstated. A fact that was not lost on anybody in the Symbolic or Connectionist camps.
It’s disputed if the Perceptrons book led to the first AI winter in the 1970s. It certainly did not help. But funding for many AI research paths dried up in the 1970s.
The Connectionist movement was vindicated in the long run. They lost the battle then, but they won the war, and the fruits of their research eventually gave us AI.
The ductility we so prize in our software and tools today is antithetical to a strict, symbolic world model spun of axioms and facts that we hoped would one day birth AI. Yet to try and give birth to this world they had to build the most ductile tools of them all: LISP and, from that, also software like Emacs. The ultimate hacker’s tool.
It is ironic then that a neural network, a crude facsimile of how a brain works, a construct that is by its nature ductile and malleable, won out in the end.
So I feel a profound sadness that I started out programming DreamCoder in Emacs, the most extensible editor in the world, by hand back in May 2025, only to see DreamCoder write itself… in DreamCoder today.
Future
I am still sad, but I also know that our industry completely reinvents itself every decade or two. This is my second career upheaval. Most programmers today have not been around long enough to go through it themselves. So I feel for them that this especially massive quake is their first encounter with how unsentimental our industry is.
But for all the sadness, I wake up every day with a feeling of optimism that I have not felt in a very long time.
I finally get to build again, no longer weighed down by my decades of knowledge and experience that held my ambition in check. I truly have not felt this liberated since I was a teenager programming in Delphi, blissfully unaware that the things I was busy building were impossible for a self-taught teenager to ever realize. I see this reflection in others: the best programmers I know also love AI. Amateurs also revel in AI’s capabilities, happy that they can finally solve problems they could never afford to pay a programmer to do for them.
I must admit that building software has, over the years, gotten a lot more complex, with an ever-larger share of that work being repetitive tedium. This is more so with hobby software – as I do not get paid to do it, so I do not have a moral duty to see it through – where I’d do all the fun bits leaving just the enervating, boring and soul-crushing parts behind. Do you have a projects folder full of sad, abandoned projects like I do?
Now I can craft in abundance. AI has freed up a lot of toil but I somehow still find myself busy all day doing real work.
Building a coding harness is perhaps the closest I will get to the optimism all those researchers and scientists must have felt in the 1970s and 1980s. They hoped that with a little bit more work, their logical rules would kindle a new intelligence. Fifty years on, and I can simply tell DreamCoder to improve itself and watch as it changes before me. I can ask the AI running inside it to analyze the changes I have made to its tools and prompt and have it adjust them accordingly. It feels like science fiction; the very thing the researchers of yesterday strove to build. Yet we really do live in this reality now.
Taste is a scarce, human resource.
So. DreamCoder. Let me address the 900 lb gnu in the room: DreamCoder is not an Emacs-related application. The reason is unfortunately one of economics and access: I want to build an AI coding harness for everyone. But don’t worry: I have some cool plans for DreamCoder + Emacs, and AI + Emacs more generally going forward. So stay tuned.
But what about all those other coding harnesses? Well, most of those harnesses all suffer from the same mistakes. It is a problem that is not unique to coding harnesses or the people who make them, but a constraint we all labor under, and one that is not easily replaced by AI:
Taste is a scarce, human resource.
And for all the bounty of AI, it still requires a human to persevere and to see things through. One thing intensive use of AI coding has taught me is that we’re going to need a lot of computer programmers who know what they’re doing going forward. I believe this is so, because let us be honest, most people do not want to program computers, even if that computer can actually do the bulk of the work for them. It requires a steady hand to build reliable software; that has not changed.
Therefore, if we programmers have to spend a lot of our time interacting with AI, then the tool we do it with should be ‘human-centric’ in its design, and it should take advantage of all the modern features we have at our disposal.
Back in May 2025 I took a look at all the tooling and said “no, thank you.” Today I look at the landscape and I feel pretty much the same.
And I think I am not the only one who feels that way. Most of these coding harnesses, to me, feel bristly. They shouldn’t be; but they are like that because we are at an important inflection point where no one really knows what the future looks like. We’re all just… fumbling around a bit. It’s an exciting time to build software, even if we don’t quite know what the world will look like a few years hence.
One thing I am adamant about is that DreamCoder must be a powerful, frontier-class coding harness. That means it should have all the features you’d expect from that: backgroundable sub agents, MCP servers, cache efficiency, and all that stuff. Check.
But that stuff quickly recedes into the background because, you know, it just works. Day to day you will dart between chats and terminals and whatnot, and you need an interface that accommodates that. Emacs is a tiling window manager; so is DreamCoder. DreamCoder’s window manager is a little bit cleverer than most window managers as every pane has a minimum, comfortable and maximum size. The window manager will therefore ensure windows always fit snugly on your screen, and you’ll never end up in a situation where windows are tiny and unreadable. It has a sophisticated constraint satisfaction solver that tries to balance your demand for a new window (“open a terminal”) with the challenge of keeping your visible panes roughly the same size. If DreamCoder can’t wedge in a new pane, it’ll punt one to the hidden window bar. Just click it to resurface it, or hover it to see what it’s doing; it’s a live view.
Because of my Emacs roots, I think a good tool must be keyboard-friendly. Because it runs on a browser you get the mouse for free of course. But smacking the tab button over and over is a frustrating user experience in complex webapps, and doubly so a tiling window manager: where exactly are you going to end up when you tab from one window to the next? To combat that, I built an avy-style window and “point of interest” selector for chats. Tap a key and pick from a selection of “embark”-like actions such as clicking links or opening pictures. It’s a work in progress, but I think it works well.
Most high-volume operations like opening and creating panes is done through a Helm-like interface with search-as-you-type. It’s really efficient, of course. And it works with a mouse also; which is sort of the point. The keyboard’s there for those who want it, and the mouse for regular folk who are just getting started. One unique feature of the design, which admittedly I am still exploring privately, is that everything is stored as Javascript objects (on account of running in your browser) so it’s not too much of a leap to build “macros” that prefill most of these dialog windows, leaving behind just the fields you want to edit.
But yeah. With DreamCoder I want to take the best of Emacs and its coterie of third-party packages and bring some of that with me. The world is still not ready for an Emacs-shaped future, sadly, so that is why DreamCoder is a standalone application and a web frontend.
Another thing that drives me wild: I see people with tmux running 10 claude codes (or codex, or…) cycling between them like a duck gallery at a carnival to see if one of them is done working, or if it needs human intervention.
So there’s two things to unpack here: one is running lots of things in parallel, and the other is observability. You need insight into what is going on: is an AI jammed because it’s awaiting an answer or a tool safety prompt? Perhaps you’ve parked a bunch of chats pending some conversations with coworkers or other work that must finish first.
In DreamCoder you have workspaces. They’re like virtual desktops (or window configurations in Emacs lingo): a snapshot view of panes as you want em. As you can see from the screenshots, panes expand to fill all the space. So if you want more space, you can: resize them (with the mouse or keyboard); shuffle them to a named workspace; or float them so they sit on top of the other windows.
But if you’ve got a lot of things happening in multiple workspaces, it’s hard to keep tabs on that. That’s why DreamCoder has a big, honking minimap in the top-right corner. One for each workspace. The minimap is a miniature of your actual layout. Each pane in the map gently pulses when it’s working, and it makes it abundantly clear when it’s blocked. When there’s nothing to do, it’s green.
Because workspaces and panes are distinct things you interact with, it must be easy to navigate between them.
I also wanted full-on, optional Emacs key bindings, but that is… pretty much impossible to properly build. Browsers lock you out of some rather important Emacs button combinations. Sadly that feature is parked until I can solve it on all major browsers without breaking your normal browser keys.
That’s not to say it doesn’t have Emacs-inspired key bindings. Most global actions are reachable with Alt+x, akin to M-x; local, pane-specific ones with Alt+c. Alt+m activates keyboard mode: you can now type the number of the named pane to jump to it; or WASD to switch the active pane in that cardinal direction.
Support for open weight models like Qwen, Gemma, Deepseek, GLM, etc. is also very important to me. They work so well. I’m really surprised, here in late 2026, just how capable small models are at local-only development compared to just one year ago. Qwen 3.8 27B, for example, is fantastically good for its size. You can do a lot of good software development with it if you’re a capable hand yourself. Bigger models equal more auto piloting; but that Qwen model? Wow. So local models work great. In fact I think the future is local for a lot of use cases. Intelligence is fast approaching a cost where it will be too cheap to meter. If you remember the personal computer revolution in the 1980s and 1990s, then there are definitely echoes of that here.
If you’ve been holding off on local models then I do recommend you reconsider. Small ones like Qwen 3.8 27B (or its cousin, Flash Next) can run well on a high-end gaming rig or Mac, or with a little investment if you do not have that. If you have a dinky old computer and you’re cash starved, then not all hope is lost. Turn to the potato agronomists on twitter: give twitter’s AI, Grok, what you have and what you can reasonably spend and tell it to track down the cutting edge setup for your rig. This is no lie the fastest, easiest way to catch up to the cutting edge of self-hosted inference today. Five minutes.
Coding harnesses are the IDEs of the future
As I’ve been building DreamCoder, I have come to the belief I’m not just building a coding harness. Coding harnesses are an IDE for the future; it will do more than just display a chat window for coding agent work. DreamCoder does more than that already. It’s going the way of Emacs in that it’ll consume a wide range of adjacent workflows and tools. But I have only just gotten started. I am brimming with ideas I’m building in parallel, but they take time because as I said it’s not about the code; it’s just one small facet of building something that works well. But you know that already: it’s always the last mile.
DreamCoder is the most ambitious, technically complex and advanced software project I have ever built in my life. And that’s just the beginning. I’m not done. I’ve barely started. I will be blogging about this going forward, in addition to my usual Emacs scribblings.
In fact, the thing I’m currently grinding away at is a world-class pentest and cybersecurity suite in DreamCoder. Every single bit of software we have ever written is vulnerable; we have many rough years ahead of us. Just look at the crippling vulnerabilities coming out every day now almost. Even the most security conscious person is going to find themselves on the wrong side for no other reason than we depend on packages that were mature and stable and assumed to be secure. DreamCoder can do its bit to help catch many of most obvious weaknesses, especially as new software is minted every day that also needs thorough testing.
To round it off, I would like to formally invite you to join me in making DreamCoder better by trying it out. It’s great. It’s not a toy; it’s not a demo; and it’s not a weekend prototype. It’s a frontier coding harness that has most of what you’d expect: MCP, backgroundable sub agents and shell commands, terminal windows, skills, hooks, 99% cache hit, it runs for days, and an interactive UI for all of it. There’s a handy dandy importer for your Pi, OpenCode or Codex configs also to help you get started. A couple of clicks and your model settings are set up in DreamCoder. Ready to go.
Please do e-mail me your thoughts ((rot13 "zvpxrl@znfgrevatrznpf.bet")) on AI, coding harnesses, what you’ve built with it, and what you think more generally about where our world is heading. I’m keen to hear from you.
And if you want to hear more from me on the technical aspects of AI, building coding harnesses, and more, then do sign up for the DreamCoder newsletter below.
